disease_info: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a trauma- and stressor-related disorder that develops following exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, either directly, as a witness, or through repeated exposure to aversive details. It is characterized by persistent re-experiencing of the trauma, avoidance of trauma-related stimuli, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and marked changes in arousal and reactivity lasting more than one month with associated functional impairment. The clinical course can be acute or chronic, with symptoms sometimes emerging after a delayed interval or becoming exacerbated by new stressors or reminders. PTSD is distinguished from other anxiety and mood disorders by the clear temporal and phenomenological link to a qualifying traumatic event and the prominence of trauma-specific re-experiencing and avoidance phenomena.

narrative.stressor: About 14 months ago, Demetrius was doing an emergency after-hours service call in an older apartment building on Cleveland’s East Side when a gas leak in the basement ignited while he and a younger apprentice were working near the furnace. The resulting explosion and fire trapped them briefly; Demetrius managed to get out with minor burns and smoke inhalation, but his apprentice suffered severe injuries and later died in the hospital. In the months that followed, he tried to throw himself back into work, church, and his community league basketball team, but he found himself increasingly unable to handle calls in older buildings, avoiding certain neighborhoods, and struggling to maintain his usual reliability on the job. When his foreman pulled him from several assignments due to safety concerns and his church mentor noticed he was withdrawing from the youth apprenticeship program, Demetrius finally agreed to see a mental health professional after his primary care doctor suggested PTSD during a visit for ongoing tension and work-related difficulties.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep seeing that explosion in my head like it’s happening all over again, and I can’t shut it off.”

narrative.stressor: Roughly a year and a few months ago, Maria flew back to Guatemala after her younger cousin, whom she had helped mentor from afar, was killed during an armed robbery on a bus. She arrived in time to help with funeral arrangements and was present when the family viewed the body and recounted the circumstances of the attack in graphic detail, with local news replaying footage of the crime scene. Returning to New York, she tried to regain her structured routine of Agile projects, salsa nights, and hikes along the Hudson, but she found that anything related to buses, crowded public transit, or news about violence in Latin America became overwhelming, and she began to pull back from community events that might bring up conversations about the incident. After her manager noted a drop in her usual engagement at work and her husband pointed out how much she was avoiding trips back to Guatemala and even planning them, she brought up her ongoing distress with her primary care provider, who referred her to psychiatry when it was clear the trauma around her cousin’s death was still affecting her life and relationships.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I go out of my way to avoid anything that reminds me of what happened to my cousin, even if it means cutting out parts of my life.”

narrative.stressor: About 13 months ago, Roy was skippering his sloop in a local race when a sudden squall rolled into the bay; a competing boat capsized nearby, and he watched a crew member get struck by the boom and thrown into the water before rescue boats could arrive. Although he and his crew were physically unharmed, the chaos of the storm, the radio calls, and the sight of the injured sailor being pulled from the water left a deep impression on him, especially given his long identification with the Cape’s maritime community. Over the following year he continued working as a project director, but his wife and sailing club friends noticed he became increasingly tense and overly reactive to minor noises or sudden shifts when out on the water, leading him to cancel several races and even avoid kayaking on days he once would have relished. When he startled so violently at a dropped tool during a woodworking class that others commented and he felt embarrassed and unsettled by how on-edge he’d become in everyday situations, he consulted his primary care doctor, who referred him for psychiatric evaluation given the persistence and impact of his trauma-related reactions.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I jump out of my skin at the smallest noises, like I’m bracing for something bad to happen all the time.”
